newsitem.title: INDIA: India SEBI mandates takeover if holding exceeds 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: India SEBI mandates takeover if holding exceeds 10 pct.

text.p: Indian market regulator the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), on Thursday said a takeover offer would become mandatory as soon as an acquirer's equity holding crossed ten percent.
SEBI said in a statement it was permitting acquirers who held more than 10 percent but less than 51 percent to make "creeping acquisitions" of two percent of stock in any 12-month period.
Any purchase by a person holding more than 51 percent would have to be made in a transparent manner, by a public tender offer, SEBI added.

"An acquirer, including persons presently in control of the company should make a public offer to acquire a minimum of 20 percent in case the conditions for a mandatory public offer...is attracted," the SEBI statement said.
In view of a lack of availability of bank finance or any other external source of finance at present, the public offer was restricted to 20 percent instead of 100 percent, it said.

SEBI said conditional offers would be allowed subject to a minimum mandatory acceptance of 20 percent with differential pricing, or with a deposit of half the value of the offer in cash in an escrow account.
The second concition would apply if the bidder did not want to be saddled with the 20 percent acquisition, SEBI said.
"This, while checking frivolous conditional offers, will permit genuine flexibility to the investor," it added.

Though SEBI will not be involved in the pricing, it specified that the pricing would be based on parameters like the negotiated price and the average of the high and low price for a 26-week period before the date of the public announcement.

Other factors affecting the pricing would be the highest price paid by the acquirer for any acquisition during the 26-week period before the date of the announcement and the price for preferential offers, if any.
SEBI said any move by the board of the target company to induct any representatives of the acquirer during the offer period would be subject to further conditions.
Neither will the board be permitted to transfer shares to the acquirer until all formalities related to the offer have been completed.

SEBI said it had reduced the scope of its discretionary powers to a minimum by delineating the cases where the regulations would be made inapplicable and by setting up a panel to consider cases for exemption.
Disclosure requirements and penalty provisions have also been strengthened, it added.
